vignette:
The event happened in the spring of 1972, when she was a field researcher in her late twenties. She had been cataloging soil samples along a remote stretch of the Oregon coast, a solo assignment that required overnight stays in a small research station. A colleague, someone she had worked beside for months and trusted, followed her to the station one evening. She remembered the way he had smiled before he pushed the door shut behind him. She had not said no, not in the way that would have mattered, and for decades she told herself that was the whole truth of it. Now, at seventy-seven, Eleanor could no longer hold that story together. The details had broken apart and rearranged themselves into something that felt more like a trap than a memory.

She lived alone in a single-story house on the edge of a small town in Washington, where the forest pressed close against her backyard. As an environmental scientist, she had spent her career reading landscapes, understanding patterns of erosion and regrowth. That same vigilance had turned inward. Every time she came home, she stood in the doorway and listened before she stepped inside. She checked the locks twice, then a third time. When she heard the furnace click on or the floorboards settle, her body went rigid before her mind could catch up. She had come to believe that safety was something she had to earn through constant watchfulness, and that the moment she let her guard down, someone would be there.

She avoided open spaces now, especially the wide, exposed parking lots of the grocery store and the medical center. She parked as close to the entrance as possible, walked with her keys pressed between her fingers, and never looked up. Eye contact had become unbearable. She had the sense that if she met someone's gaze, they would see something in her—the shame she carried in her body, the knowledge of what had happened—and she would be exposed all over again. When a male colleague at the environmental agency asked her to review a report in his office, she said she preferred email. She never explained why. She simply began to schedule her work hours so that she was never alone in a room with a man.

Physical affection had become impossible. Her sister, who lived two hours away, had tried to hug her goodbye at a family gathering last Thanksgiving. Eleanor had stepped back, her hands raised, and said she was feeling unwell. She had felt the confusion in her sister's face, and the guilt had sat in her chest for days. But what frightened her most was the way her own body reacted—the sudden cold, the urge to flee, the sense that she was about to be pinned down again. She had come to believe that her body was a liability, that it had betrayed her once and would do so again.

She thought constantly about how the event could have been prevented. If she had locked the station door. If she had not smiled at him that morning. If she had driven back to town instead of staying the night. The rumination was a loop that played behind everything she did, and she could not find the off switch. She had told herself for years that she was fine, that she had built a good life, that the past was the past. But the PCL-5 score of 73 told a different story. She had finally come to a therapist because her doctor had noticed the weight loss, the sleeplessness, the way she flinched when a nurse touched her shoulder. Eleanor had agreed to come, but she was not sure what she hoped for. She was certain that no one could undo what had happened to her body. She was afraid that if she told the whole story out loud, she would never stop hearing it.
